title: Statements and expressions
intro: In Rust the pieces that steer a program, `if`, `match`, loops and `{ }` blocks, are expressions: they produce a value. The last line of a block, with no `;`, is the block's value, and a function's last line is what it returns.

coming_from.go: `if` and `switch` are statements in Go, so you declare `label := "odd"` first and assign inside a branch. In Rust `if` and `match` give a value, and a function ends with its result, written without `return` (`return x;` still works). `a = b = c` and `if x = 1` fail in both languages, for different reasons: Go's assignment is a statement, Rust's is an expression worth `()`.
coming_from.kotlin: You already have `if`, `when` and a lambda's last expression as values, and Rust works the same way. The new parts: a Rust function body in braces also returns its last expression (Kotlin needs `return`, or the `= expr` form, which Rust does not have), a bare `{ }` is a block, not a lambda, and assignment is an expression worth `()` where in Kotlin it is a statement. `a = b = c` fails in both.
coming_from.python: Python ends a statement at the newline; Rust ends it at `;`. A bare `x + 1` line in Python is worked out and thrown away, and so is `x + 1;` in Rust. A line with no `;` at the end of a block is the block's value. A Rust function declares its result type, so a body that ends `x + 1;` instead of `x + 1` is a compile error, not a quiet `None`.
coming_from.typescript: `c ? a : b` becomes `if c { a } else { b }`, and a `switch` statement becomes a `match` that gives a value. An arrow function with braces needs `return`; a Rust function or closure in braces returns its last expression, like `x => x + 1` does without braces. `a = b = c` and `if (x = 1)` compile in TypeScript; in Rust they are type errors.
coming_from.java: Rust has no `?:`; `if` is an expression, so it is not needed. `match` is like the Java 14+ `switch` expression. A method returns its last expression with no `return`. Java lets assignment sit inside an expression (`a = b = c`, `if (flag = true)`); Rust does not.
coming_from.csharp: `?:` becomes `if c { a } else { b }`, and `n switch { ... }` becomes `match n { ... }`. Rust has no `=>` expression body: a function uses braces and returns its last expression. C# lets assignment sit inside an expression (`a = b = c`); Rust does not.
coming_from.c: Rust has no `?:` and no comma operator: `if` is an expression, and `{ f(); 2 }` is a block that gives 2. `if (x = 1)` compiles in C (gcc warns only with `-Wall`); in Rust the condition must be a `bool` and an assignment is worth `()`, so it is an error. A non-`void` C function that runs off its end is a problem only if the caller uses the result; in Rust it is a compile error.
coming_from.cpp: Rust has no `?:` and no comma operator: `if` is an expression, and `{ f(); 2 }` is a block that gives 2 (standard C++'s closest is an immediately called lambda). `if (x = 1)` compiles in C++ (gcc warns only with `-Wall`); in Rust it is an error. Running off the end of a function that returns a value is undefined behaviour in C++ even if the caller ignores the result; in Rust it is a compile error.

notes: The last expression in a block, with no `;`, is the block's value. It is called the tail expression. Put a `;` after it and the value is thrown away: the block is then worth `()`, Rust's "nothing" value.
`if`, `match`, `loop` and `{ }` can all sit on the right of `let` or be the last line of a function. Every branch must agree on a type (a branch that leaves, like `continue`, fits any type).
`return` is for leaving early. At the end of a function, write the value without `return` and without `;`.
Assignment (`x = 5`) is an expression, but it is worth `()`, so `a = b = c` does not chain and `if x = 1` is a type error. Conditions must be `bool` and need no parentheses.

gotcha.title: A semicolon on the last line
gotcha.looks_fine: Most languages you know end a statement with `;` or a newline, and a function ends with `return x + 1`. A function whose last line is `x + 1;` looks finished: only the word `return`, which Rust does not need, seems to be missing.
gotcha.rust_sees: `x + 1;` is a statement: the sum is worked out and thrown away. The block then has no final expression, so its value is `()`, and the function promised an `i32`.
gotcha.why: One character changes what a line is. With the `;` it is a statement. Without it, it is the block's value. Rust cannot guess which you meant, so it points at the `;` and says to remove it. Look at the other languages' results: most refuse, Python quietly returns `None`, and C and C++ compile with warnings and give an undefined result.

go.says: Go refuses twice: `x + 1` is "not used", and there is a "missing return". The fix is `return x + 1`. Go has no last-expression rule.
go.error:
# command-line-arguments
./main.go:6:2: x + 1 (value of type int) is not used
./main.go:7:1: missing return

kotlin.says: Kotlin refuses with "missing return statement". A block body needs `return x + 1`; the other fix is the expression form `fun addOne(x: Int) = x + 1`.

python.says: Python runs this and prints `None`. The body computes `x + 1` and discards it, and a function with no `return` gives back `None`. Nothing complains.

typescript.says: TypeScript refuses (TS2355): a function declared to return `number` must return a value. The fix is `return x + 1;`.
typescript.error: main.ts(1,29): error TS2355: A function whose declared type is neither 'undefined', 'void', nor 'any' must return a value.

java.says: Java refuses: `x + 1;` is "not a statement", because Java only allows calls, assignments and a few others as statements. The fix is `return x + 1;`.
java.error:
Main.java:3: error: not a statement
        x + 1;
          ^
1 error

csharp.says: C# refuses twice (CS0201 and CS0161): `x + 1;` cannot be a statement, and not all code paths return a value. The fix is `return x + 1;`.
csharp.error:
Program.cs(3,5): error CS0201: Only assignment, call, increment, decrement, await, and new object expressions can be used as a statement
Program.cs(1,12): error CS0161: 'AddOne(int)': not all code paths return a value

c.says: gcc compiles this. With the runner's `-Wall -Wextra` it warns twice (plain `gcc` says nothing) and the program prints 41. `x + 1;` is legal C. The problem is the missing `return`: using the result of a call that ran off its end is undefined behaviour. On this runner (ARM64, no `-O`) the argument `41` is still in the register the caller reads the result from. With `-O1` or higher the same program printed 0. If the caller ignores the result, C runs fine.
c.warnings:
main.c: In function ‘add_one’:
main.c:4:7: warning: statement with no effect [-Wunused-value]
    4 |     x + 1;
      |     ~~^~~
main.c:5:1: warning: control reaches end of non-void function [-Wreturn-type]
    5 | }
      | ^

cpp.says: g++ compiles this with warnings, then the program crashes before printing. In C++, reaching the end of a function that returns a value is undefined behaviour even if the caller ignores the result. Here g++ put a trap instruction at the missing `return` (SIGTRAP, exit status 133; with `-O2` the same program segfaults instead).
